subtype: Approach: spending impulsively at the first temptation [Pitfall]
passage:
“Pranav, why is there a shoebox on your bed?” Rekha didi asked.
“Sale. Half price. It ended in an hour, so I just bought them.”
“With what money?”
“The bicycle money.” He nudged the box with his foot. “But they're really good shoes.”
“How much was in the tin?”
“Three thousand one hundred. Now it's two thousand one hundred. Wait.” He counted on his fingers. “That's two more months of saving, isn't it?”
“At your weekly amount, yes. Two months.”
“I didn't even need them. Mine are fine.”
“What would have happened if you'd waited a day?”
“I'd have looked at the tin and not clicked buy.”
“Then stick a note on the tin: sleep on it before buying.”
Pranav groaned, then reached for a pen.

qa.q: How much money is left in the tin?
qa.a: Two thousand one hundred is left in the tin.

qa.q: What is Pranav feeling as he counts on his fingers?
qa.a: Pranav feels regretful and a little sheepish, since he admits he didn't even need the shoes.

qa.q: What could Pranav do to stop impulse buys in future?
qa.a: He could sleep on it for a day before buying, as the note on the tin says, since the urge fades and the goal stays in sight.

qa.q: How might Rekha didi feel about the purchase?
qa.a: Rekha may feel concerned yet supportive, since she asks questions instead of scolding and offers a simple note rule.

grounding: A teen with saved money buys shoes on impulse at an online sale, and the bicycle goal is set back by two months.
